titleStmt.title: Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, and Machine Learning: A Transformative Symbiosis in Favour of Financial Technology

analytic.title: Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, and Machine Learning: A Transformative Symbiosis in Favour of Financial Technology

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper uses a multidimensional descriptive analysis to familiarize the reader with the extent of penetration of big data, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) techniques in the financial technology roadmap. We propose a clear framework for the symbiotic nature of these data science themes towards fintech empowerment. The framework is validated through their impact in fintech, financial services' profession and the shifting paradigm of the data scientist role. We also discuss the dark side of this symbiosis, while AI and ML techniques are tied with the future challenges of AI ethics, regulation technology and the smart data utilization.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Financial Technology (fintech) is a contemporary topic that has been in the centre of recent developments in the finance industry and a subject of an emerging research strand. This abbreviation is frequently cited in the same context of terms such as innovation, disruption, revolution, big data analytics, blockchain inter alia. However, navigating through its landscape is not easy. To do so, researchers such as Arner et al. (2015) follow a fintech timeline that starts before the 1970's. In particular, the authors explain that the transition from analogue to digital services (Fintech 1.0: 1886(Fintech 1.0: -1967) ) is the first manifestation of fintech principles. This period is the prelude for developing and expanding the required infrastructure for enabling globalized financial services. The installation of the first ATM by Barclays in 1967, and the establishment of NASDAQ and SWIFT institute in the 70's mark the era of Fintech 2.0 (1967 -2008), which mainstreams the use of digital banking and online customer services. Within these decades, the world came across electronic trading floors, personal finance applications and high-frequency trading. These advances have been revolutionary at the time and have shaped financial market operations till now. The above shows that it is a misconception when the public associates fintech with the cryptocurrency hype after 2009. We thus observe a transition to Fintech 3.0.

The post-financial crisis infused the lack of trust in banks and brought the democratization of financial services to the forefront of the debate. This debate was originally shaped around regulatory changes and technological advances (e.g., smartphone adoption, Banking as a Service (BaaS) platforms, Distributed Ledger Technology, inter alia).

The fintech hype is evident over the last decade, but recently even more. Why now? Goldstein et al. (2019) answer this question by suggesting that the fusion between technology and financial services is more enabled now due to the high pace of adoption of new technologies. This fusion originates mostly from outside the financial industry, through startups and big tech companies disrupting banks' business models and their traditional competitive advantage in financial services products. The financial world is gradually evolving into a digital domain of high-volume information and high-speed data transformation and processing. The more this transformation takes place, the more consumer and investor behaviours shift towards a protechnology attitude of financial services offered by market participants, financial institutions, and financial technology companies. Fintech solutions nowadays take the form of a service, software, or business decision-making tool that allows financial processes to be more efficient in terms of cost and speed, while consumers are further empowered by selecting from a variety of options better tailored to their needs and financial circumstances. The effect of this is that traditional financial institutions become gradually unpopular, and their operations get disrupted and disintermediated. We take the arguments of Arner et al. (2015) and Goldstein et al. (2019) one step further, and we postulate that fintech is more 'exotic' now than ever, because of the gradual acceptance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques in finance along with the availability of big data after the Internet-of-Things and Web 2.0 revolution of the last decades. These three elements are 'breadcrumbs' within Fintech 3.0. However, their symbiosis can lead to a fintech transformation in the years to come, namely Fintech 4.0.

This symbiosis is tethered because digital technologies enable entrepreneurial activity and expand its scope (Nambisan, 2017;Chalmers et al., 2021), and boost fintech empowerment (Siau et al., 2018). AI automation and ML efficiency are the main technological tools to harness and leverage the information power from big data pools concentrated in servers of financial institutions and firms. This confirms that fintech innovation and disruption of traditional financial services are steered through information technology advances (Hauswald and Marquez, 2003). These two pillars of the data analytics discipline are found to be the main technology of choice for key participants in the financial markets aiming at improving security, reducing operating costs and smoothing business processes, and more importantly, providing robust financial analysis results for decision making. Academic findings such as the above are also supported by practitioner reports. For, example Accenture (2017) states that fintech is more about 'tech', than 'fin', implying that improvements in financial services would not be possible without the emergence of new technologies such as AI and ML. McKinsey Global Institute (2018) also identifies a fintech company as a start-up that applies technological advances to impact the way consumers behave in terms of their basic financial operations (e.g., savings, borrowing, investing, payments and protection).

To motivate our study, we showcase the transformative fusion between big data, AI, and ML through some examples from the fintech sector. Battling financial fraud is an example of significant success from the side of AI. AI-based agents are very efficient, particularly in identifying malicious transactions related to e-commerce and credit card online transactions (Ryman-Tubb et al., 2018). The success is based on the systematic and automated analysis of location, transaction history, and shopping habit data of credit card users through ML algorithms.

For example, open-banking operators such as Plaid use this as a major selling point for their digital financial services. AI and ML solutions are also highly successful in credit decisionmaking. Their main advantage over traditional credit scoring systems and underwriting processes is that they are cost-and time-efficient and, at the same time, less restrictive and more transparent. ZestFinance and Ocrulus are typical platforms offering such credit scoring and lending management solutions. Finally, AI and ML techniques offer better customer targeting and retention platforms. One major success of the fintech industry is attracting and displacing GenZ customers from traditional financial institutions. The implementation of robo-advisors through ML agents is the key driver of this success. Moneybox and Mylo APIs are representative cases of how millennials can be persuaded towards saving and investment and eventually become more financial literate. Big data analytics and gaining strategic value from the extrapolated information are common denominators for all case studies mentioned above. This paper contributes to the related literature by providing a comprehensive review of how AI, big data, and ML have been shaping the future of fintech. Other studies, such as Lee and Shin (2018), discuss the historical evolution of fintech and assess that fintech creates disruptive innovation capable of changing business models and investment types in financial markets.

Recently, Liu et al. (2020) review the 629 research papers on fintech business models, and find that mobile payment, microfinance, peer-to-peer lending platform and crowdfunding are the essential research topics over the period 1995-2017, while future studies will look at blockchain and crowdfunding. We take a distinct approach that differs from such studies in that we combine insights and findings from academic research, professional surveys, and regulatory perspectives. To date, several attempts have been made to review and synthetize the state of the art of the fintech ecosystem and research (e.g., Lee and Shin, 2018;Milian et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2020), but little is known about the effects of AI and ML in conjunction with big data on the fintech evolution and applications. Another important strand of literature focuses more on the impacts of fintech on financial markets, instruments, and services (e.g., Chang et al., 2020;Boot et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2021a). Although our work ties with that literature too, to the best of our knowledge, this paper is the only study that attempts to shed light on how the fusion of big data, AI, and ML occurs in the fintech domain. In that effort, a novel conceptual framework is provided to highlight how these three data science pillars manifest symbiotic characteristics that have a transformative effect for the fintech sector.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 presents some interesting descriptive statistics on AI, big data, and ML techniques and illustrates their symbiotic characteristics towards fintech. Section 3 presents a non-technical summary of big data, AI, and ML in relation to the development of fintech. Section 4 discusses the relevant AI and ML landscape, describes its impact in conjunction with big data analytics. Section 5 concludes the study with some remarks on the future challenges of big data, AI, and ML within the fintech roadmap.
Further technical information and statistics are provided in an online appendix.

div.head: Big data, AI and ML in Fintech: 'May the force be with you'!
div.p: Fintech is the new paradigm in the financial markets and the banking industry. To comprehend this shifting ground in the field, Capgemini (2018) survey is ideal. Figures 1 and2 below summarize the results of the survey.

div.head: [Insert Figure 1-2]
div.p: The figures outline a strong belief of senior banking executives that FinTechs are disrupting domains traditionally ruled by financial institutions, such as payments, savings, and even loan or mortgages. The survey also illustrates that banks need to foster collaboration with FinTechs towards creating new services, transforming the bank into a platform, and opening and exchanging their customer base with each other, rather than attempting to develop new services in-house. This is the new pathway towards generating non-traditional revenue streams worldwide. In a sense, senior banking executives realize that a new digital culture needs to be adopted, and innovation needs to be promoted and fostered internally. That requires a major shift in the strategic priorities of the financial institutions. The optimal strategies outlined in Figure 2 shows that financial institutions need to become more adaptive, agile, and fast in embracing change and technological innovation while enabling and supporting incubators is also high in the list of strategic operations. Even the factors that appear lower in the list, such as IT transparency and operation openness, are important shifts in traditional banking perceptions.

For example, Chen et al. (2019) claim that the Internet of Things (IoT) is an important driver of fintech innovation. This development is further supported by increased investment in fintech (KPMG, 2019) and shifts in consumer behaviour (EYFIN, 2019).

All the above underline the true nature of the fintech revolution and the disruption and disintermediation that traditional banks face. However, it is not exactly clear how big data, AI and ML are intertwined to the fintech narrative. For that reason, we next present some relevant information and statistics that bring information technology and the above techniques in the spotlight. First, big data analytics could be defined as the complex, time-and computing-consuming process of examining large and varied data sets. Their motivation is to uncover unknown information, patterns, trends, correlations, and potential customer preferences that enable businesses with robust decision-making tools. Big data, per se, are anecdotally connected with the notion of storage and analysis, while they are characterized by volume, velocity, variety, and veracity. This is the so-called 4 V's framework in computer science (Lozano et al., 2020). Their importance for the fintech revolution is anecdotal and can be illustrated Cisco Systems Inc. (2018). The report clearly shows an exponential trend in increasing big data storage in data centres and most importantly a shift towards increasing growth of internet traffic inwards or outwards to business-end users. This is shown in Figure 3.

div.head: [Insert Figure 3]
div.p: These practitioner results corroborate the findings of Chen et al. (2019) who prove that fintech innovation is gradually driven by big data, including financial services. 1 However, if we do not observe equivalent important results on AI and ML with fintech, the main analytical tool of big data, it would be difficult to prove their symbiotic nature.
For that reason, we turn towards AI and ML as an enabling technology for financial services.

The recent advances in AI and ML create a paradigm shift in every sector of the tech industry due to their ability to cope with high dimensional datasets. This is an integral part of the digital transformation of financial services (De Madro, 2018;Jagtiani and Lemieux, 2019;Jakšič and Marinč, 2019;Kraus et al., 2020). To support the previous finding and probe AI/ML utility in fintech, we need to explore their benefits extrapolated from different perspectives (e.g., economic impact, patents, software, hardware, investment). By reviewing the academic literature and practitioner reports, Table 1 summarizes our findings.

div.head: [Insert Table 1]
div.p: It seems practitioners and consultancy firms agree on the importance of AI and ML across all themes with academics. However, academic research appears to be concentrated more on investment analysis and general economic impact evaluation. Few academics focus on fintech innovation through patent fillings and software and hardware design innovation. Regardless of this, it is obvious that AI/ML are in the forefront of fintech. Additionally, it is very easy to prove the symbiotic nature between them through Figure 4.

div.head: [Insert Figure 4]
div.p: 1 IDC (2018)'s report on the size of data utilized in different industries in 2018 is also supporting the importance of big data in fintech. Particularly, financial services join manufacturing and retail industries to the top three ranked data-driven sectors. There is a myriad of relevant big data, AI and ML statistics that for the shake of space are not presented in the main text. For more information, we refer the interested reader in our online appendix A.

ML applications and platforms remain the main driver of AI investment. This is in line with the fintech trend, as advances in ML have a prominent spot in various financial applications and financial services' operations (Aziz et al., 2021). Finally, ML applications remain a focus point when it comes to digital payments, supply and demand predictions and online customer engagement and data security. All these elements are key strategic goals for financial institutions that are digitally transformed and aim not to alienate their customer base (Vives, 2017;Thakor, 2020). ML and AI solutions should create revenue boosts and cost reductions if they are considered transformative for fintech. McKinsey Analytics (2019) concludes that AI and ML provide meaningful value to these domains from a cost/revenue perspective. These gains are expected to be extrapolated by AI applications in marketing and sales, product and service development and supply-chain management. 2The fintech 'cosmos' is generally constructed around some institutional pillars. Jofre (2016) and his new 'world order' summarize them as banking, capital markets, private equity, regulation, and technological innovation. Those 'galaxies', except the latter, are stagnant and static for long time. In that spirit of space parallelism and connecting with the known blockbuster movies' quote3 , we position AI and ML as the 'force' keeping the galactic balance in the fintech universe. However, some academics err on the side of caution. Buckley et al. (2019) discusses the dark side of digital financial transformation, focusing on the risks extrapolated from information technology and big data analytics. Gligor et al. (2021) also share concerns about business-to-business relationships that can be negatively affected by these trends. Taken all the above into account, we are motivated to investigate further whether the compatibility of big data, AI, and ML can have transformative power over fintech, for the better or worse.

div.head: Big data, AI and ML 'universe': A non-technical summary
div.p: Following the fintech context and the information relevant to big data, AI and ML of the previous sections, it is now appropriate to provide a summary of the techniques, with a non-technical and understandable approach for the mainstream 'fintech reader'. Practically, the three domains can be easily summarized in Figure 5.

div.head: [Insert Figure 5]
div.p: ML, as a subset of AI, is the medium that empowers the penetration of AI science in the big data analytics domain. What exactly is the big data analytics domain, though? In order to provide a relatively accurate answer to this question, we need to discuss how big data analytics differ from other methods of analytics. The easiest approach is by comparing traditional analytics associated with business intelligence approaches. Traditional methods of analytics are based on descriptive diagnostics, utilize limited 'cleaned' datasets with simple statistical models. They are generally structured and repetitive processes focusing on causation. On the other hand, big data analytics are based on predictive techniques, utilize raw, large-scale and multidimensional datasets with complex modelling. Their results are experimental and 'ad-hoc', while their processes are semi-structured, randomized and aim at unravelling unknown correlations and new insights through data mining, rather than causal effects. In terms of size, traditional analytics results do not exceed the size of some terabytes (TB), while their big data counterparts can reach sizes of hundreds of petabytes (PB). 4Big data are characterized by the 4 V's, mentioned earlier. In order a dataset to be classified as big data needs to combine volume (data that are static and ready for processing, e.g., customer credit history), velocity (data that are in motion and change very quickly, e.g., social media information), variety (data in many forms, e.g., text, multimedia) and veracity (data in doubt, e.g., databases with inconsistencies, completed with latency or missing values). Rice (2020) provides some contemporary examples of big data. The most notable examples are discovering consumer shopping habits, personalized marketing, monitoring health conditions through data from wearables devices, media streaming, real-time data monitoring and cybersecurity protocols. Academics have attempted to simplify and summarize the notion of big data in fintech through several survey studies (see, e.g., Wang et al., 2016;Fang and Zhang, 2016;Ennouri and Mezghani, 2021;Cong et al., 2021;Goldstein et al., 2021). Financial institutions are top producers of structured and unstructured data, hence banks are expected to be leaders in the big data domain. Examples of banking big data are real-time stock market insights, adaptive market and consumer sentiments, fraud signalling, and risk analysis based on high frequency financial and market information. Big data analytics' techniques are the only available method to provide the fifth V in this framework, namely value. In other words, techniques such as AI and particularly ML can provide approximations on how much value is created from each unit of data for the task at hand and identify potential contributions of subsets of the data to the problem's solution. The more data complexity rises, the more potential for incremental business value exhibits itself through such techniques5 .

Attempting to define the term AI is not easy. There is no consensus on what an ideal definition would be. From a philosophical perspective, intelligence itself is a difficult notion to define (Monett and Lewis, 2017). Expectedly, when this notion is expanded to non-mainstream topics that the general public cannot follow, such as the realm of algorithms, automation and robotics, this task becomes more challenging. Wang (2019) is attempting to define AI starting from a variety of different perspectives. The fact that this manuscript is over 30 pages speaks volumes for the difficulty of the task. Starting from the father of AI, John McCarthy (Andresen, 2002), AI is the "science and engineering of making intelligent machines". This intelligence, artificial in nature, is enabled by advances in computer science and approximated by studying and designing intelligent agents, who can understand their environment and make decisions that maximize success for each given task. These AI agents are expected to cope with multi-dimensional ideas, learn from past data, apply statistical inference, tackle complexity and ambiguity presented by large scale datasets, and finally make speedy efficient responses. Main branches of AI are pattern recognition, heuristics, genetic algorithms, neural networks and ML (see amongst others, Bishop, 2006;Angstenberger, 2013;Groner et al., 2014;Kasabov, 2019;Molnar, 2019). AI could also be broken down into four components of applications, namely expert system design, heuristic problem solving, NPL operations and image or visual identification. The integral base for all these applications is the ability of AI to learn and improve performance without the need for a human interaction, namely the ML capability. Bahrammirzaee (2010) provides a seminal summary of AI in Finance, while more recent attempts are available by Adadi and Berrada (2018), Veloso et al. (2021), andBayramoğlu (2021). The latter attempt to reapproach the topic by looking into the 'black-box' delivering interpretable AI examples. The delivery of a detailed topology of AI's evolution over the last decade is not the main scope of this study. However, the interested reader should refer to the online appendix B.

When attempting to understand ML, we need to differentiate between different segments of the techniques in order to position their utility in the big data analytics domain. In particular, Supervised Learning (SL), Unsupervised Learning (UL), Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Deep Learning (DL) methods should be part of the discussion. The selection of each learning method is decided by the type of research question at hand along the available data. Assuming X input variables and a Y output variable, a learning algorithm can be used to obtain a mapping function F. In other words, we want to approximate the following relationship Y=F(X). The goal of ML is to calculate F so accurately, so when new input data X are made available, the predicted values of the new Y are very close to the actual ones. The SL or UL differentiates depending on the use of prior knowledge. If we know the correct answers (which means that we have fully labelled datasets during the training process), we can directly interpret the accuracy of the results. This would be a case of SL. Classification and regression problems are commonly solved with SL and techniques such as logistic regression, support vector machines, neural networks and random forest algorithms (see, e.g., Sermpinis et al., 2017;Zhou et al., 2019;Katuwal et al., 2020;Smyl, 2020). Having such perfect datasets, though, is not always possible, while given the big data discussion above in most cases SL can easily become impractical. This is where UL comes in place. When the output variable Y is not available, then the weight shifts towards the identification of the natural structure of the available data. In other words, the expert system does not hold the 'right answer'. The UL algorithm is supposed to find out what the input variables X show to the best of its ability. That is why UL techniques are suitable for clustering, anomalies detections and density estimations. Typical methods for UL are nearest-neighbour mapping, k-means clustering and singular value decomposition (Hastie et al., 2009;Shen et al., 2011;Chen and Hao, 2017). In both SL and UL, the learning process is terminated once a specific threshold of performance is reached.

RL algorithms are meant to train an intelligent agent or machine for making decisions, which through trial and error yield the higher rewards (Sutton and Barto, 2018). This learning framework involves the agent, its environment and the potential action set. The goal is to reach the maximum expected reward over a specific time limit. In other words, the machine is learning to obtain the best policy, given the data available and the rewards and penalties each action imposes. Although the reward policy is in a sense supervised, the algorithm has the freedom to maximize the reward by leveraging the power of search and random trials. That is why within the huge realm of ML algorithms, RL is bridging the gap between computation and cognition in the most efficient way (Collins, 2019). DL techniques are employing multiple layers to gradually extract higher level of features from the raw input dataset. The most common models are the Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Gu et al., 2018) inspired by the natural visual perception mechanism of the living creatures. They are able to learn unsupervised from data that is unstructured or unlabelled, while they are particularly capable in image recognition. The online appendix B presents a more detailed topology of ML methods and their relevant applications.

Naturally everyone is puzzled to a certain extent about how the interaction of big data, AI and ML is formed and transformed along with the recent advances in the data science. Mayo (2017) intuitively attempts to revisit this puzzle, as in Figure 6.

div.head: [Insert Figure 6]
div.p: Mayo (2017) claims that although big data remain crucial in data science, they become less important as a separate entity. Only the transformative symbiosis of AI, ML and DL can move big data analytics steps forward. They will be the driving force for solving this riddle, creating different avenues towards cognitive technologies and increasing 'black-box' interpretability, while they will add value for investors, data analysts and computer scientists. The mainstream public and old-fashioned businesses need to reconcile with the fact that these techniques are here to stay and, given the fintech environment, become gradually accessible and attenable in a form of service or product. All the above present a basic and 'painless' picture of how big data, AI, and ML universe is structured. Next, we delve deeper in the way their symbiotic characteristics can transform fintech.

div.head: Fintech transformation through big data, AI, and ML
Fusion of big data, AI, and ML: A conceptual framework.
div.p: In order to show the transformational power of AI/ML/big data for fintech, we initially formulate a conceptual framework that ties big data, AI, and ML with the fintech landscape. Initially, we follow Imerman and Fabozzi (2020) in formulating the roadmap of fintech innovation. This is summarized in Figure 7.

div.head: [Insert Figure 7]
div.p: The respective fintech ecosystem is split into traditional fintech segments (fintech verticals) and traditional operations and applications (fintech horizontals). The horizontals are split to traditional financial services functions (functional areas) and technology innovations. These emerging technologies are dominated by big data, AI, and ML or advanced derivatives of them and their efficient combination (APIs, Cloud and Quantum computing, Cybersecurity, Automation inter alia). 6 We connect the previous with the 'supply-demand' framework of the Financial Stability Board (FSB, 2017) as shown in Figure 8.

div.head: [Insert Figure 8]
div.p: While the fintech verticals appear as the main supply factors in this transition, they are tied also with most of the demand factors. FSB (2017) also provides further drivers of fintech innovation through AI, such as capital and investment optimization, trading and portfolio management, model risk management and bank stress testing. This is also related to the work of Hasan et al. (2020) that explain that the role of big financial data is very prominent, unlike in other non-financial disciplines. This signs off the idea of a nested relationship between big data and AI/ML within financial services. However, there is the last dimension to our conceptual framework. This is related to the balance between economic interpretability, data complexity and computational scalability as illustrated in Figure 9.

div.head: [Insert Figure 9]
div.p: Understanding such trade-offs is crucial if the transformative power of big data, AI, and ML is captured efficiently. Interpretable economic analysis from small scale datasets convinces less and less policymakers, economists, investors and particularly financial and government institutions, who are the big data generators. Reconciliation between financial economics' research and operational research expertise is thus needed to obtain causal interpretation of 'black-box' models and the fusion to be achieved (Zhao and Hastie, 2019;Holm, 2019).

div.head: Impact on the fintech sector
div.p: Our analysis of the impact of big data, AI and ML on fintech aims to follow the fintech horizontals identified before. Setting of this effort from the big data perspective, Hasan et al. (2020, p.7) present an overview of research on big data and related emerging financial factors.

As outlined by the authors, there is extensive literature linkage between big data analytics and studies across different financial applications (financial markets, credit risk, financial growth, risk management, fraud detection, internet finance, financial analysis, inter alia). Their findings are crucial in our quest, as it is common for the non-fintech mainstream reader to disassociate big data with pure financial services and focus only on user-generated content in social media, environmental measurements, and other types of big data. These is clearly not the case as In terms of digital banking and mobile payments, Navaretti et al. (2018) explain that fintechs disrupt the digital payment domain and impose profit loses for traditional banks, but the latter are better at bundling this service segment with other banking activities (e.g., lending, investing and savings). For that reason, a shifting paradigm is observed, where fintechs' business model is becoming more banking-focused, while traditional banks transform to technology incubating institutions. Thakor (2020) claims that the main fintech disruption to banking is going to be associated with peer-to-peer (P2P) lending, smart contracts and cryptocurrencies. This disruption is expected to manifest more prominently in financially developed countries where financial literacy and inclusion is higher. Recently, Ma and Fildes (2020) propose a third-party mobile-payment platform for daily payment forecasting through ML solutions (e.g., the Gradient Boosting Regression Tree) method and empirically validate its robustness. AI and ML promote fintech substantially through credit scoring and lending by harnessing the information power of big data. Agarwal (2019) suggests several ways that these data science techniques can impose change. The operational research and finance literature is extremely voluminous on this part (Lessmann et al., 2015). The AI research on credit scoring goes back to studies of 1992 (Jensen, 1992), as the first evidence of their role in Fintech 2.0.

Since then, researchers such as Ong et al. (2005), Marques et al. (2013), Ala'raj and Abbod (2016), and Goh and Lee (2019) bring forward the methodological success of AI and ML techniques in credit scoring decisions. Aziz et al. (2021) apply topic analysis to show that credit scoring forecasting is the most frequent topic in the field of ML financial application.

The picture is similar when it comes to lending, but the applications are somewhat less extensive than credit scoring. Ye and Cho (2014) propose a hybrid model of heuristics and ML for P2P, while Metawa et al. (2017) discuss the use of genetic algorithms for optimizing bank lending operations. Ma et al. (2018) suggest that LightGBM and XGboost algorithms are successful in predicting P2P loan defaults. More advanced deep learning techniques also perform very well in the same domain (Kim and Cho, 2019). These are further supported by the work of Tang (2019) on P2P lending market., while Bastani et al. (2019) present an overview of the techniques as in Table 2.

div.head: [Insert Table 2]
div.p: The authors suggest that the use of deep learning can improve P2P lending decisions and at the same time cope with the class imbalance problem between non-default loans (being the majority) and default loans (being small in numbers). Traditional manual credit assessment can, therefore, be substituted with ML methods coping with unstructured and time-adapting data. These methods are able to leverage qualitative information (e.g., consumption patterns) and past credit history without violating well-accepted bank policies.

Another important effect is improvements in financial fraud detection and prevention (Vasant and Litvinchev, 2020). In the context of the Internet of Things (IoT), financial fraud is usually associated with unauthorized mobile transactions through mobile devices or online platforms. The current state of advances in AI and ML are providing a very solid framework for institutions in identifying fraudulent transactions. The imposed SL and UL algorithms become part of an expert system that predicts fraudulent behaviour through historical data and is usually combined with traditional investigative approaches in case available data are not enough for robust predictions. DL methods are gradually becoming complementary methods in these expert system designs. Ryman-Tubb et al. (2018) survey the impact of AI and ML in payment card fraud detection, and they perform a very comprehensive ranking of AI methods in this segment, outlining their transformative power for financial services. The authors summarize the AI fraud detection segment with the ontology in Table 3.

div.head: [Insert Table 3]
div.p: A third dimension of AI applications is use virtual assistants and aiming at creating exceptional customer experience and reducing call centers' personnel costs. We have discussed in previous sections the growth of chatbot industry in relationship with automated call centers as driver of fintech disruption. Statista reports that the AI call center market revenue is expected to exceed $930 and $740 million in North America and Europe respectively. Another survey from Statista, conducted to more than 1000 US residents between 18 and 65 years old, explains that 22% of the respondents would like to use digital voice assistance when communicating with insurance companies. This ties well with another fintech segment, where AI and ML are found to be successful. Hall (2017) explains that insurers utilize AI as a tool for customer experience improvement, enhancement of sale and services execution, faster claim processing and accurate individual risk-based underwriting processes.

The extension of robo-advisors for wealth management is also crucial to explain the fusion between big data, AI, and ML. The use of robo-advisors for portfolio management (Park et al., 2016) is a recent literature trend. For example, Phoon and Koh (2017) provide easier and quicker access to digital loans through AI-based robo-advisors, while Xue et al. (2018) show that ML techniques provide solid investment decisions through classification. Recently, Shanmuganathan (2020) reports impressive performance in of Robo pioneers such as Wealthfront and Bettermen (e.g., two-year annualized return of more than 5%)7 . Crowdfunding is another pillar of AI in fintech, although academic research is not as extensive. Several researchers investigate the success of such projects through ML applications. Wang et al. (2020) prove that Deep learning methods demonstrate potential for crowdfunding project financing predictions. Yeh and Chen (2020) find similar results. Recently, Behl et al. (2021) provide a theoretical framework on how the adoption of AI tools enables donation-based crowdfunding and boosts operational performance. Big data and AI act further as enablers of this fintech empowerment, as they provide solutions for enhanced and targeted marketing (Wierenga, 2010), increase sales revenue with AI-based Customer Relationship Management (Gantz et al., 2017) and, finally, cybersecurity amplification (Truong et al., 2020).

Academics in the fields of quantitative finance, econometrics and OR are leaders in empirical research with big data, ML and AI hybrid techniques (Sermpinis et al., 2017;Tashiro et al., 2019;Gu et al., 2020,). This trend has expanded especially within the cryptocurrency forecasting domain (Atsalakis et al., 2019;Chen et al., 2021b). Financial ML and OR were the 'black sheep' of academia before 2010. Since then, traditional econometrics and financial economic techniques fail to cope with immense dataset sizes and turn to AI and ML methods (Bahrammirzaee, 2010;Cavalcante et al., 2016;Ozbayoglu et al., 2020). The topic analysis reveals such prominent themes of shown in Figure 10.

div.head: [Insert Figure 10]
div.p: Finally, insurance decision-making and real estate valuation are also transformed through big data and AI. This is the message brought forward by studies such as Baudry and Robert (2019), Corea (2019), Viriato (2019), and Starr et al. (2020). Overall, the impact of big data, AI, and ML is documented across all fintech segments outlined in our conceptual framework.

div.head: The impact on Fintech-related professions
div.p: These are examples of professions that are expected one way or another to heavily interact with fintech related advances. Not surprisingly, several of these fintech related professions are deemed to be affected by the disruption imposed through technological innovation. It is wellaccepted in the labour literature that skill-biased technology shocks can impact unemployment and labour market decompositions (see, e.g., Mortensen and Pissarides, 1999;Graetz and Michaels, 2017;Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2018). Specifically, León-Ledesma and Satchi (2019) suggest that the technology frontier of firms determines jointly how the balance between capital and labour is shaped. Appropriate technology innovation provides a pathway to sustainable growth, but with different short-term and long-term effects for employment decisions.

Assuming that firms' long-term growth is a true expectation of big data, AI and ML technological advances (as described in previous sections), it is crucial to map the challenges, benefits and ramifications that they bring forward for the fintech professional terrain.

McKinsey Analytics (2019) survey provides important insights on the effects of AI adoption in the worldwide workforce balance across different industries. Financial services' AI related workforce is expected to observe an eroding effect. Consumer packaged goods and transport and travel services workforce is projected to further expand in 2020-2023. The same survey suggests that firms classified as high AI performers are promoting large scale retraining of their workers. 8 The World Trade Report (2017) explains that the 4 th industrial revolution based on smart technology, AI and algorithmic modelling would potentially impose job losses but also new job-creating opportunities. Nonetheless, AI advances disrupt different industries disproportionally, hence governments and policy makers should consider these asymmetric effects seriously in order to avoid the risk of the so-called 'jobless future' (Ford, 2015).

Focusing on financial analyst and accounting profession, AI advances provide robust decision-making tools for investment, growth and confidence in the operational process and business challenges that these professionals aim to smooth and solve. The main benefit is their ability to exploit larger datasets and obtain effective metrics and measurements towards correct allocation of business resources without increasing lack of accountability or the risk of ineffective audit. The ICAEW, which is committed to advancing the theory and practice of accountancy, discuss these elements in their report 'Artificial intelligence and the future of accountancy'.9 More specifically, it is explained that the ML techniques can provide solutions across all accounting tasks. Traditionally accountants apply technology to extract insight from data analytics, usually in a SL framework. This leads to improvements of cost allocations, detection of fraudulent financial reporting and enhancement of strategy development for businesses. In other words, they are a parallel function of business analytics. The use of AI in accountancy enables certified public accountants to shift their attention from monotonous manual tasks to making more analytic and data -driven decisions (Jaslove, 2017). Additionally, advances in accounting and auditing are tied with the application of expert systems designed on the principles of ML forecasting and fuzzy logic decision making (Omoteso, 2012;Dickey et al., 2019).

Generally, financial services professions seem to be reinventing themselves through the proliferation of big data, AI and ML. It is no more the static professions they used to be, at it is embracing automation and technological innovation. The cloud computing is transforming the respective workforce into digital advisors that can streamline workflows and extract unseen commercial insights. At the same time, they can promote paperless and sustainable processes, avoid time consuming back-ups and impose high levels of security (Kwilinski, 2019;Yau-Yeung et al., 2020).

div.head: Data scientists in fintech: The AI and ML labour shifting paradigm
div.p: Another manifestation of the transformative synergy of big data, AI, and ML in favour of fintech is how the demand and employability of data analysts and software developers have skyrocketed in financial services. Although data scientists are a flexible workforce in terms of industry placement, most fintech-related professions converge to skillsets originated in data analytics and computer science. Figure 10 and 11 paint the true picture about the AI/ML labour market.

div.head: [Insert Figure 10-11]
div.p: Interestingly, AI/ML-related jobs remain top four in ranking both in future growth and salary bumps. Additionally, quantum computing -a by-product of advanced ML for big data analytics -appears first (Shaikh and Ali, 2016). Other surveys complement this picture by highlighting the role of computing, AI/ML, and Devops as high-impact technology trends for organizations. 10 The figures support our conceptual framework in terms of supply and demand in the technology labour market. This is clearly related to the need of financial services and organizations to cope with data whose complexity increases exponentially. According to O'Reilly's 2016 Data Science Salary Survey, 45% of the those surveyed that hold the title of data scientist, are involved in a huge variety of business intelligence and growth relating tasks. 11 Except from expected tasks such as data analytics, data cleansing and prototype developing, data scientists play a huge part in communicating findings to upper management and identifying opportunities and challenges for their firm. The survey reports that they also collaborate in team projects and mentor younger staff, while assisting in fostering external relationships and developing consumer products. These are functions traditionally attributed to the role of manager or business strategist. María Cavanillas et al. ( 2016) investigate the new horizons for a data-driven economy. They explain that there are new big data opportunities in the finance and insurance sector.

To explain the link between data scientists and these new horizons, they map potentially relevant research questions with their technical requirements and the big data technologies that can be applied. This is summarized in Figure 12.

div.head: [Insert Figure 12]
div.p: In conclusion, the symbiosis of big data, AI and ML techniques transforms data scientists into an amalgamation of tech savviness, expert knowledge-based modelling, digital entrepreneurship, modern marketing and customer retention force. Hence, data scientists seem to be a perfect fit for the 'Data-Driven Fintech Framework' proposed by Gai et al. (2018). This presents a labour shifting paradigm in the fintech labour market. Following up on the title 'Rise of the machines' of the work of Chaboud et al. (2014), we witness the 'rise of the data scientists' 10 DevOps is a set of practices that combines software development and IT operations. Examples of such surveys is the Vanson Bourne and Nutanix ones in 2019 available at www.statista.com. 11 The survey is available at: www.oreilly.com/radar/2016-data-science-salary-survey-results. The detailed outline of the data analysts tasks are provided in online appendix D.
in the era of fintech. If someone wants to understand the fintech revolution in depth, this is the fountain of disruption or the 'force' that we hope to be with us!

div.head: The dark side of the 'force': Theoretical and practical aspects
div.p: As highlighted above, our initial suggestion of the transformative coexistence of big data, AI, and ML favouring fintech advances holds. However, this fusion is powerful and, in some cases, difficult to control. In other words, harnessing this symbiosis in favour of fintech can lead to the dark side and overleverage the given opportunities, which without any doubt raises concerns of theoretical and practical nature.

From a theoretical point of view, many studies investigate these concerns based on automation narratives, such as 'AI degrades human ability', 'AI decreases jobs availability', 'AI lacks of accountability' and 'AI reinforces bias' (e.g., Pomerol, 1997;Gurkaynak et al., 2016;Kumar et al., 2019;Ashta and Herrmann, 2021;Hassani, 2021). More recently, Gligor et al. (2021) present an interesting theoretical framework around the dark side effects of organizational relationships. The authors associate overleveraging AI and big data analytics with social dominance, organization inertia and organizational information processing theories. The main message of harnessing AI and big data can be a double-edge sword. As apart from the known advantages, data scientists can become the dominant partners in the organization, make only resource-based decisions, lack creativity, and foster inertia forces within financial services. Boot et al. (2021) discuss such challenges in fintech and explain that data generation and ownership is a major hurdle. The authors explain that big data are often undefined, but they present economies of scale and scope. Therefore, there is an incentive for unregulated exploitation and the avoidance of 'data monopolies' from financial institutions is crucial. Finally, Chalmers et al. (2020) theorize around the AI relationship with digital entrepreneurship. Although AI augments entrepreneurial activities, the authors suggest that they present liabilities of technological leverage, such as growing inequality, labour displacement, and algorithmic bias.

From a practical perspective, avoidance of the dark side is tied with a 'preparedness/concern' trade-off applied across fintech. Deloitte (2020) develops this framework which is summarized in Figure 13.

div.head: [Insert Figure 13]
div.p: The evidence provided could be considered as a dire picture and support the prior theoretical discussion. Issues related to cybersecurity, AI failures, and data breach liabilities are fields of major concern. Thus, the big data, AI, and ML symbiotic nature can have transformative power even towards the 'dark side' of fintech.

div.head: Concluding remarks: Future challenges, AI ethics, Regtech and Smart Data
div.p: This article attempts to provide a framework under which a mainstream reader interested in digital technology, entrepreneurship, and fintech-related professions can understand why the fintech revolution is tied with the advances in big data analytics, AI and ML. Initially, we deliver some multi-dimensional statistics on AI, big data, and ML techniques and show their symbiotic characteristics towards fintech. Then, we present a short non-technical summary of big data, AI, and ML concerning the development of fintech. The main body of the study proposes a clear framework for the fusion of big data, AI, and ML towards fintech empowerment.

Financial services' segments through supply and demand factors with the trade-off between economic interpretability, data complexity, and computing scalability. This framework is validated with evidence of their impact on fintech, financial services professions and roles of data scientists as a labour powerhouse in the field. We also discuss the dark side of this symbiosis through the lens of academic theories and practitioners. The latter provides a segue from this point to the future of AI and ML in fintech.

There are several challenges that the fintech future bears with the evolution of intelligent agents, automation and algorithmic modelling. These could be categorized into three dimensions. The first is related to the ethical challenges AI brings to the spotlight in the context of fintech. Ethical considerations about the use of machines are well documented (Bostrom and Yudkowsky, 2014;Hagendorff, 2020). An Emolument survey reports that 47% of financial services employees believe technology can put their job at risk, while McKinsey Global Institute (2018) forecasts that automation can crop around 30% of the hours worked globally by 2030, especially in the financial services sector. Customer interaction in financial services is also another sector affected by AI takeover. Assuming these expectations are remotely accurate, then ethical challenges related to digital privacy, artificial intelligent bias, lack of accountability and morality become very apparent. The compliance to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) framework is thought to keep AI ethical (Franklin, 2019), but most expert audiences are not convinced. The Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) software predicts the likelihood of recidivism in criminal defendants and is a perfect example of such AI bias and lack of accountability. Israni's New York times op-ed12 claims that there is no transparency in the way COMPAS works as the manufacturer does not disclose their algorithm design. This fact does not deter judges from using COMPAS score in sentencing, despite propriety claims creating a responsibility-free net for the AI designer. COMPAS has also been accused of racial profiling and reiterating wrong crime-related stereotypes (Washington, 2018). So, the question is if similar AI-based investment platforms mishandle investments and incur capital losses, who is responsible? Can the firm employing this algorithm claim that they did not have a role in this 'accident' and to what extent are they responsible for the damages? These are not easy questions to answer at this stage of the fintech revolution.

That is why regulation technology, the so-called regtech segment, is crucial for the fruition of information technology in the financial sector. Regtech emphasizes on regulatory monitoring, reporting and compliance and it is expected to play a leading role in making fintech acceptable to the general public, policy makers and regulators. Ernst and Young company explain that many organizations invest a huge amount of money and time in order to cope with compliance, audit, regulation and reputation risks. The use of appropriate technological advances, such as AI and ML, can make this process cost effective and robust, especially when it comes to regulation monitoring, identity verification, activity and transaction monitoring and compliance registers. Fintech and regtech interact in many dimensions (Arner et al., 2016;Anagnostopoulos, 2018) and create a new realm of opportunities for banking institutions and firms 13 . A very important aspect of this interaction is the compliance with national and international regulations, such as the Patriot Act, the Bank Secrecy Act and the EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives. In short, fintech's future success is tied to the level of transparency regtech is expected to bring.

The data science puzzle also needs to be revisited along with the evolution of big data to smart data (Luengo et al., 2020). The ability to generate big data characterized by the 4 V's was documented before. Smart data, on the other hand, are the structured or unstructured data that are filtered in an efficient way in order to provide the value, the fifth V. Smart data collection can be very challenging. They are expected to create value from lower volume of information, need to be faster and used in real-time scenarios and decision-making processes. This adaptive nature, although approximated by DL methods and other ML variants, is not yet achieved to its fullest potential. The advances of combining these methods with the power of GPUs seems to provide very high data processing speeds. But this is not enough to achieve the transition to smart data. Business priorities and strategies need to evolve through the input of data scientists. Often organizations, in their inability to clean and understand the true value of the data collected, create data swamps incurring high data storage costs without having an accurate picture of their quality, quantity and format. The transition from big data to smart data goes through cleaning these data swamps and transforming the data warehouses into 'data 13 The regtech landscape is so vast that it should be in the scope of a separate study. Nonetheless, we refer the interested reader to online appendix D for a short illustration on what regtech capabilities for IT operations, risk management, business continuity inter alia. lakes'. The above are confirmed by NewVantage Partners' survey14 , which identifies lack of organizational alignment and cultural resistance to change as the biggest challenges of big data adoption among corporations. Inability to view big data as the true business asset also appears to be major challenge. In conclusion, this study's main message is that big data, AI and ML 'force' is strong in fintech. It is up to financial services' professionals, regulators, policymakers, government institutions and educators to foster it, rather than turn to its 'dark side'…
